questions.question: Compare spores and seeds, and give two reasons why seed plants can live in drier places than mosses and ferns.
questions.expected_answer: A spore is a tiny reproductive structure, usually a single cell, with almost no food store and no protective coat; a seed contains an embryo (young plant), a food store and a protective seed coat. Seed plants can live in drier places because seeds can survive drought and wait to germinate when conditions improve, and because their male sex cells are carried in pollen by wind or animals, so they do not need water to swim to the female cells.

questions.question: Describe the main features of mosses and ferns and explain how ferns reproduce.
questions.expected_answer: Mosses: small, no true roots (anchored by rhizoids), stems or leaves, no transport tissue, grow in damp shady places, reproduce by spores released from capsules, need water for sex cells to swim. Ferns: true roots, stems (often rhizomes) and leaves (fronds), with transport tissue so they can grow larger; spores are produced in sori on the underside of fronds; a spore grows into a small plant that produces sex cells, which need water to meet, and the fertilised cell grows into a new fern.

questions.question: Distinguish between gymnosperms and angiosperms and give two South African examples of each.
questions.expected_answer: Gymnosperms (naked seeds) have no flowers; their seeds develop exposed on the scales of cones, and pollen is usually carried by wind; examples: real yellowwood, Outeniqua yellowwood, cycads (Encephalartos), and introduced pines. Angiosperms (seeds in a container) have flowers; the ovary develops into a fruit that encloses the seeds; pollen is carried by wind or animals; examples: protea, aloe, mealie, marula, acacia, grasses.
